step1_summary: Chief complaint: 4–5-day history of worsening sore, red, very itchy, dry skin rash.

Symptoms: Pruritic erythematous patches on chest, hands, arms—worst on antecubital fossae; skin cracking but no weeping/exudate; no fever, joint pain, breathing issues; aggravated by scratching; no clear alleviating factors reported.
Past medical history: Chronic eczema (atopic dermatitis); asthma.

Medications/allergies: Daily emollients (Diprobase cream, Dermol shower wash); OTC hydrocortisone cream; PRN blue asthma inhaler; previously tried OTC antihistamine (cetirizine) without benefit; no known drug allergies.
Family history: Mother with hypothyroidism and migraine.
Social history: Lives in London; no smoking/alcohol history mentioned.
Vital signs/exam: Virtual visit—no vitals; visual description only—diffuse erythematous, dry, non-weepy rash with fissures, no lichenification, no scratch marks, no thickened hyperpigmented skin.

V: Small-vessel cutaneous vasculitis: Could present with widespread erythematous lesions, but absence of palpable purpura or systemic symptoms makes it less likely.
I: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare: Chronic history, classic distribution (flexural surfaces), pruritus, dryness, recent exacerbation.
Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis: Acute worsening; could be triggered by new environmental exposure even if patient unaware.
Scabies infestation: Generalised pruritus, commonly involves wrists and flexor surfaces including elbows.
N: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides): Chronic eczematous patches resistant to therapy could mimic eczema.
D: Nutritional deficiency dermatitis (e.g., niacin deficiency—pellagra): Can cause dermatitis in sun-exposed areas but pattern and history less suggestive.
I2: Drug eruption (exanthem, DRESS, etc.): No new medications reported, but always a consideration if any recent OTC or herbal products.
C: Ichthyosis vulgaris: Congenital dry scaly skin, but patient reports acute change.
A: Psoriasis (guttate or plaque): Erythematous patches, but lack of silvery scale, distribution and personal history favor eczema.
T: Mechanical irritation/dermatitis from friction or scratching: Could worsen existing eczema.
E: Endocrine (thyroid) related xerosis: Hypothyroidism can cause dry skin, but not acute red pruritic flare.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Patient has known eczema with classical distribution and symptoms; common to have episodic flares that become more widespread/pruritic.
supporting_evidence: Documented history of eczema treated with emollients and hydrocortisone.
Typical flexural involvement (antecubital fossae) with dry, erythematous, pruritic skin.
Absence of systemic signs of infection; no weeping or exudate.
opposing_evidence: Current topical regimen not controlling symptoms—could suggest alternative or superimposed condition.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute worsening could be triggered by new product/exposure; presentation overlaps with eczema.
supporting_evidence: Sudden flare over a few days, more severe than usual.
Distribution includes chest and arms that may contact clothing, detergents, etc.
opposing_evidence: Patient denies any change in skin products or routine.
Chronic history of similar rashes favors endogenous eczema.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Severe itching with predilection for flexural areas could indicate scabies, particularly if family or close contacts symptomatic.
supporting_evidence: Intense pruritus; involvement of hands, wrists/antecubital area.
opposing_evidence: No mention of nocturnal predominance, burrows, involvement of finger webs or household contacts.
Rash described as dry patches rather than papules or nodules typical of scabies.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Can present with erythematous patches; stress can precipitate.
supporting_evidence: Erythematous rash involving extensor and other areas.
opposing_evidence: Lacks characteristic silvery scale, well-demarcated plaques; patient history points to eczema.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Generalised erythematous rash could be medication induced.
opposing_evidence: No new medications or recent drug change reported.
